title: TCP — The Reliable Delivery Protocol
description: Understand how TCP guarantees reliable data delivery through handshakes, sequence numbers, acknowledgments, and flow control.

segments.text: Last time we saw data flying across the internet. But here's the thing — the internet is unreliable. Packets get lost, arrive out of order, or show up duplicated. TCP fixes all of that.
Before any data is sent, TCP establishes a connection using a three-way handshake. Think of it like a phone call — you dial, the other person picks up, and you confirm you can hear them.

Step one: the client sends a SYN packet — 'I want to talk.' Step two: the server replies with SYN-ACK — 'Got it, I'm ready too.' Step three: the client sends ACK — 'Great, let's go.' Connection established.
Now, this handshake adds latency — one full round trip before any real data moves. That's the cost of reliability.
segments.thought_prompt: Why might this round-trip cost matter for applications serving users globally?

segments.text: Once connected, TCP assigns a sequence number to every byte of data. If you send a thousand bytes, each one is numbered. This lets the receiver reassemble data in the correct order, even if packets arrive scrambled.

The receiver sends acknowledgments back — 'I got bytes up to number five hundred, send me the rest.' If the sender doesn't get an ACK in time, it assumes the packet was lost and retransmits it automatically.

Retransmission is TCP's safety net. It uses a retransmission timeout that adapts to network conditions. Slow network? Longer timeout. Fast network? Shorter timeout. TCP learns the rhythm of your connection.

But what if the sender is too fast for the receiver? TCP handles this with a sliding window. The receiver advertises how much buffer space it has — 'I can handle sixteen kilobytes right now.' The sender respects that limit.
Flow control protects the receiver. But what about the network itself? Congestion control prevents TCP from flooding the pipes. It starts slow, ramps up, and backs off when it detects packet loss.
This is called slow start followed by congestion avoidance. TCP doubles its sending rate until it hits trouble, then grows linearly. It's a brilliant balancing act between speed and safety.
segments.thought_prompt: Why does TCP use exponential growth initially but switch to linear growth after detecting congestion?

segments.text: When the conversation is over, TCP closes the connection gracefully with a four-way handshake — FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK. Both sides confirm they're done. No data left behind.

TCP gives you reliability on an unreliable network — handshakes, sequence numbers, acknowledgments, retransmission, flow control, and congestion control. It's the backbone of the web. Next up, we'll look at DNS — how your browser even finds the server to connect to.
